name: Attention Residue
summary: The mental carry-over effect where thoughts from a previous task linger and interfere with focus on a new task.
explanation:
Attention residue is the part of your attention that stays on a previous task after you switch to a new one. Sophie Leroy coined the term in 2009 while asking why it is so hard to focus on the work in front of us when we keep moving between tasks.

In her experiments, people who switched away from a task they had not finished kept thinking about it and performed worse on the next task. A surprising result: people who finished the first task under time pressure showed less residue and did better on the next task than both those who left it unfinished and those who finished it without time pressure. The likely reason is that a deadline pushes us to close the task in our heads, not just on paper. In a 2018 follow-up with Theresa Glomb, she found that expecting time pressure when returning to an interrupted task increases residue, and that writing a one-minute ready-to-resume plan before switching reduces it.

The mechanism connects to older findings. Unfinished tasks stay active in memory (the Zeigarnik effect), the previous task set keeps interfering with the next one (task-set inertia), and making a concrete plan for an unfinished goal quiets it (the plan-making effect).

Why it matters: context switching costs more than the switch itself. Every half-finished task, message you glanced at, or project you "keep an eye on" leaves residue that follows you into the next block of work, and at the end of the day it blocks psychological detachment. Practical consequences: finish or explicitly park a task before switching (write down where you are and what comes next), batch shallow work, reduce self-interruptions, keep few projects active at the same time, and close the workday with a shutdown ritual.

Caveat: the core studies were lab experiments with about 80 undergraduates each. The idea is well grounded, but the exact size of the effect in real work is uncertain.

articles.title: Why Is It So Hard to Do My Work? The Challenge of Attention Residue When Switching Between Work Tasks
